name: Absolute Negator Determinatives

t.curious: Negative words that stand in for a noun phrase
t.child: Negative words that stand in for a noun phrase

name: Absolute Supplement

name: With Plus an Absolute Predication

t.child: With plus a thing and how it is

name: Abstract Numeral Construction

name: Activity Weak Definite

t.curious: The bus that isn't a particular bus
t.child: The bus that isn't a particular bus

name: Adjectival Passive

t.curious: Describing a state with a word like locked
t.child: Describing a state with a word like locked

s: A word that looks like part of a passive verb can instead describe how something is.
x: The door remained locked. | The door remained locked. | The door remained locked. | The door remained locked. | The window remained closed.

name: Raising with an Adjectival Predicative

t.curious: Likely to, said of a whole situation

s: With a word like likely, the sentence judges a whole situation rather than describing the person it starts with.
p: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + be + PredComp:AdjP[Adj + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]]

name: Adjective
s: Adjectives are words like tall, wooden or happy that say what something is like, and they don't all behave alike.

name: Adjectival Tough Construction

t.curious: Easy to follow, hard to find fault with

s: In some sentences the adjective judges the opening noun by what we do to it, as in impossible to follow.
p: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + be + PredComp:AdjP[Adj + to-infinitival Clause with non-subject gapᵢ]]
x: Their argument was impossible to follow. | His performance was easy to find fault with. | The instructions were hard for us to follow. | Their argument was impossible to follow. | His performance was easy to find fault with. | The instructions were hard for us to follow. | Their argument was impossible to follow. | His performance was easy to find fault with. | The instructions were hard for us to follow.

name: Have with a Past-Participial Predication
s: Have plus a noun phrase and a past-participle word presents an outcome as arranged by, or happening to, the subject.

name: All Modifier Restricting a Role

t.curious: All as a restriction, as in an all girls' school

p: Nom[all + class-denoting nominal or adjective + N]

name: All of with a Stated Magnitude
s: Putting all of before a stated amount draws attention to that amount, as if it were noteworthy.

name: Singular Agreement with an Amount Expression

name: Anaphoric Not with an Attitude Predicate
s: After a word like hope, not can stand in for a whole statement, the negative of something just raised in the conversation.
x: “Is the screen broken?” “I hope not.” | “Is the screen broken?” “I hope not.” | “Is the screen broken?” “I hope not.” | “Is the screen broken?” “I hope not.” | “Is it raining?” “I hope not.”

name: Anaphoric So with an Attitude Predicate
s: After a word like think, so can stand in for a whole statement mentioned in the conversation.

name: Additive Another before a Measure or Cardinal

name: Ordered Auxiliary Chain

t.curious: Helper verbs in a fixed order

name: Auxiliary-Stranding VP Ellipsis

name: Past Perfect Anteriority

t.curious: Had plus a verb for what came earlier
t.child: Had plus a verb for what came earlier

s: Had with a past-participle verb puts an event before another moment in the past.

name: Institutional Bare Singular
s: Some everyday nouns, such as school, can appear with no article when they refer to an activity or status.

name: Bare Singular Noun Coordination

name: Bare Role Construction
s: Words like treasurer or captain can describe the role someone holds without a word like the or a in front.

name: Verbal Be-Passive
s: In a passive sentence, the object of the matching active sentence becomes the subject, and the active sentence's subject can come later after by or be left out.

name: Bare Deictic Calendar NP
s: Words like this, last and next before a day or calendar period say when something happens, measured from now.

name: Cardinal Determinative
s: A number word such as three or twenty-six can come before a noun and say how many there are.

name: Cardinal Noun

t.curious: Number words that act as nouns

s: A number word can name a number, label one thing or stand for a quantity, behaving like an ordinary noun.
x: Ten is even. | a ten | Room 101 | hundreds of people | Ten is even. | a ten | Room 101 | hundreds of people | Ten is even. | a ten | Room 101 | hundreds of people

s: In a sentence like I'll have Jo check the figures, the speaker arranges for someone else to do the checking.

name: Causative and Inchoative Alternation

t.curious: A change with a cause, and without one

name: Caused-Motion Construction

t.child: Making something move with a verb

s: In this dictionary a clause is a group of words built around a verb and what goes with it, with or without a subject.

s: Some short phrases carry the meaning of a whole statement even though they contain no verb.

t.child: Questions with a fixed set of answers

s: After a verb like wonder or ask, if can introduce a question that the sentence reports.

t.curious: Singular group nouns with plural verbs

s: A singular noun for a group, such as committee, can sometimes take a plural verb when the members are in mind.

s: A plural number word after in or by can tell how people or things are grouped.

name: Multiplicative Measure Comparison

t.curious: Moving a part to the front

s: Part of a sentence can be moved to the front to tie the sentence to something already in the conversation.

t.child: Active-looking words with a passive meaning

s: After verbs like need, an -ing word can have a passive meaning even though it looks active.

name: Constituent Negation with not

t.curious: Saying not about one part of a sentence

s: Not can deny one part of a sentence, such as a description or a time, instead of the whole action.

s: Adding away and at to a verb presents an activity as sustained or repeated, aimed at a target.

name: Coordination

s: Adding -ity to an adjective can name the quality it describes, sometimes changing how the word sounds.

name: Degree
s: English has a few ways to say where something sits on a scale, such as taller than, the tallest and as tall as.

name: Degree-Adjective-Indefinite (Big Mess Construction)

t.curious: How big a mess, too big a problem

s: With words like how, too, so, that and as, the adjective can move in front of a or an.
x: How big a mess was it? | He's not that good a teacher. | It was too big a problem to ignore. | She's so good a student that she skipped a year. | It's not as big a deal as you think. | I've never seen so big a crowd. | It's not that big of a deal. | more interesting a job than I thought | How big a mess was it? | It was too big a problem to ignore. | She's so good a student that she skipped a year. | It's not as big a deal as you think.

name: Deictic Here or There with Inversion
s: Starting a sentence with a stressed here or there, then the verb, points out something arriving, present or leaving.
p: Clause[stressed locative here/there + V + full NP], or here/there + pronoun + V

name: Deitality

t.curious: Words that behave like this and that

s: This dictionary uses deitality for a pattern of grammatical behaviour shared by the, this, that and similar words, separate from what they mean.
p: Structural profile over determination: there-resistance + partitive domain establishment + identificational hosting
x: *There was the dog in the yard. | two of the dogs / *two of some dogs (true partitive) | that idiot Larry | two of the dogs | that idiot Larry | two of the dogs | that idiot Larry

name: Delayed Right Constituent in Coordination

t.curious: One ending shared by two halves

s: In a linked pair of phrases, the shared last part can be said once, at the very end.
p: coordination[XP₁ ... gap + Coordinator + XP₂ ...] + shared right-edge constituent
x: She knew of but never mentioned the proposal. | I am interested in but worried about the new plan. | She knew of but never mentioned the proposal. | I am interested in but worried about the new plan. | She knew of but never mentioned the proposal. | I am interested in but worried about the new plan.

name: Demonstrative Determinative in Fused Determiner-Head Function

t.curious: This and that standing on their own

s: Words like this and that can stand alone as a whole phrase, pointing to something in the situation.
x: That is incredible! | That is incredible! | That plan is strange. | That is incredible! | That is strange.

name: Deictic Demonstrative Determination
s: This, that, these and those direct attention to something and can present it as near or far.
x: Could you pass me that blue folder over there? | Could you pass me that blue folder over there? | I'll take these shoes. | Could you pass me that blue folder over there? | I'll take these shoes. | Could you pass me that blue folder over there? | I'll take these shoes.

name: Demonstrative with an Oblique Genitive
s: A demonstrative plus a phrase like of Mary's can pick out a person or thing through a relation, even when only one fits.
x: that husband of Mary’s | those green eyes of Mary’s | that nose of his | that husband of Mary’s | those green eyes of Mary’s | that nose of his | that husband of Mary’s | those green eyes of Mary’s | that nose of his

name: Denominator Numeral Construction
s: A number word can work like an ordinary noun, naming an instance of a number such as a score.
x: I rolled a ten. | She drew three tens. | That's a perfect ten. | I rolled a ten. | She drew three tens. | That's a perfect ten. | I rolled a ten. | She drew three tens. | That's a perfect ten. | I rolled a ten. | She drew three tens.

name: Depictive Secondary Predication

t.curious: Saying how someone or something was at the time
t.child: Saying how someone or something was at the time

s: A word added after the verb phrase can tell you what state someone or something was in during the action.
p: Clause[primary VP + secondary AdjP/NP predicated of a participant]
x: They carried the patient unconscious. | They carried the patient unconscious. | She ate the fish raw. | They carried the patient unconscious. | She ate the fish raw. | She ate the fish raw. | They carried the patient unconscious.

name: Descriptor + Identifier Label

t.curious: A kind of thing plus its label

p: NP[descriptor + identifier: number, letter name, or alphanumeric code]
x: Room 302A, Multipurpose Room A | in Gen Z | Room 302A, Multipurpose Room A | in Gen Z | She's in Ward 17. | Room 302A, Multipurpose Room A | in Gen Z | Ward 17

name: Determination

t.curious: Words that open a noun phrase

s: A noun phrase can start with a small word or phrase that marks it as a complete phrase and signals whether we mean a particular thing or not.
x: the new car | one new car | Ally's new car | what size hat | over 20 times | the new car | one new car | Ally's new car | what size hat | over 20 times | the new car | Ally's new car

name: Deverbal Adjective in -able
s: In its central pattern, adding -able to a verb gives an adjective that says something can have that action done to it.
p: Adj[verb base + -able], with related forms in -ible
x: The document is searchable. | A dependable source is hard to find. | The document is searchable. | A dependable source is hard to find. | The document is searchable. | A dependable source is hard to find.

name: Deverbal Noun in -er

t.curious: Nouns made by adding -er to a verb
t.child: Nouns made by adding -er to a verb

s: Adding -er to a verb gives a noun for someone or something tied to that action.
x: the reviewer of the manuscript | a mixer | the reviewer of the manuscript | a mixer | the reviewer of the manuscript | a mixer | A singer stood on the stage. | Dad used a mixer for the cake.

name: Deverbal Noun in -Ing
s: Some words in -ing name an activity or its result and behave like nouns, taking words like careful and of.
p: N[verb base + derivational -ing] with nominal dependents
x: The careful sorting of the files took hours. | The careful sorting of the files took hours. | The careful sorting of the files took hours.

name: Deverbal Noun Of-Argument
s: A noun made from a verb can be followed by of and a phrase naming someone or something involved in the event.
p: NP[(Det) + deverbal Nom + PP[of + argument NP]]
x: the failure of Washington Mutual | the arrival of the guests | the destruction of the city | the death of the king | the enemy's destruction of the city | a repainting of the hall | the failure of Washington Mutual | the arrival of the guests | the destruction of the city | the death of the king | the enemy's destruction of the city | the arrival of the guests

name: Difference Complement after Different
s: The word different can be followed by a phrase that names what something differs from.

name: Measure Differential in a Comparative

t.curious: Saying how much bigger, in numbers

s: A measurement placed before a comparison word, such as wider, says by how much the two things differ.

name: Direct Quotation with Reporting Predicate
s: A direct quotation presents words as the speaker voiced them, set against a frame saying who spoke.
p: quotation + reporting predicate or reporting predicate + quotation
x: “I’ll call tomorrow,” Jo said. | “I’ll call tomorrow,” Jo said. | Jo said, “I’m ready”. | Jo said that she was ready. | “I’ll call tomorrow,” Jo said. | “I’ll call tomorrow,” Jo said. | Max said, “I’m hungry”.

name: Directive Had Better
s: Had better recommends a course of action and often hints at a bad result if it isn't followed.
x: You had better bring the receipt. | You had better bring the receipt. | You had better take a coat. | You had better bring the receipt. | You had better bring your coat. | We had better leave now.

name: Directive-Ostensive Construction

t.curious: Shouting a noun phrase to point something out
t.child: Shouting a noun phrase to point something out

s: A speaker can call attention to something present or about to happen by saying just a noun phrase, such as The bus!
x: The robbers! | Robbers! | A snake! | That man! | Your keys! | Fire! | The bus! | The robbers! | Robbers! | A snake! | That man! | Your keys!

name: Dispositional Middle
s: A sentence with an ordinary verb can describe how an action can be carried out on something.
p: Clause[Theme Subject + active transitive-capable V + optional ease/manner modifier]
x: This fabric washes well. | The fabric was washed at noon. | This fabric washes well. | The fabric was washed at noon. | This fabric washes well.

name: Distributive Rate with Each or Apiece
s: Words like apiece and each after an amount say the amount applies to every item or person in a group.
p: measure or counted NP + each/apiece, with a group supplied by context
x: The tickets cost six dollars apiece. | The tickets cost six dollars apiece. | The pens cost two dollars each. | The tickets cost six dollars apiece. | The pens cost two dollars each. | The tickets cost six dollars apiece. | The pens cost two dollars each.

name: Ditransitive VP (Double-object Construction)
s: Some verbs can be followed by two noun phrases in a row, such as someone who receives and the thing received.
x: I sent Sue a copy. | She told him the truth. | She baked Kim a cake. | I'll do you a quiche. | They refused Kim permission. | They charged Ed ten dollars. | It cost Mel his job. | I sent Sue a copy. | She told him the truth. | She baked Kim a cake. | They charged Ed ten dollars. | It cost Mel his job.

s: A word ending in -wise at the start of a sentence says which aspect the rest of the sentence is about.
x: Cost-wise, the smaller van is better. | Cost-wise, the smaller van is better. | Price-wise, the first offer is better. | Cost-wise, the smaller van is better. | Price-wise, the first offer is better.

name: Postverbal Durational Long

t.curious: Asking or denying "long" after a verb

s: Plain long after a verb works in a question, a negative or an if-clause to describe a potentially long time.
p: VP[... + long in a non-affirmative duration frame]
x: Did you wait long? | They didn’t stay long. | Did you wait long? | They didn't stay long. | Will they stay long? | They stayed too long. | Did you wait long? | They didn't stay long. | Will they stay long?

s: Each followed by of and a known group says something about every member of that group.

name: Correlative Either and Or

t.curious: Offering two choices with either and or
t.child: Offering two choices with either and or

s: Either at the start and or between marks a pair of alternatives.
x: Pick either the blue folder or the red one. | Pick either the blue folder or the red one. | You can have either tea or juice. | Pick either the blue folder or the red one. | You can have either tea or juice. | Pick either the blue folder or the red one. | You can have either tea or juice.

name: Emphatic Polarity Response Family

t.curious: Adding force to yes and no

s: Informal speakers put an emphatic word in front of yeah, yes or no to give the answer extra feeling.
p: hell + yeah | shit + no | fuck + {yeah, yes, no} | fucking + {yes, no} | hell fucking no

name: Adjective in -Ful
s: Adding -ful to a noun gives an adjective saying something has or displays what the noun names.
x: The chair gave a thoughtful reply. | The chair gave a thoughtful reply. | The colourful kite flew high. | The chair gave a thoughtful reply. | The colourful kite flew high. | She gave a thoughtful answer. | The colourful kite flew high.

name: Sufficient Degree Enough with an Infinitival
s: Enough after a describing word says that a quality reaches the level needed for a stated result.

name: Epistemic Modal over Perfect

t.curious: Judging the past with must have
t.child: Judging the past with must have

s: A modal verb of judging, followed by have and a past participle, assesses an earlier situation from a later point of view.
x: It must have rained last night. | It must have rained last night. | She may have left already. | It must have rained last night. | She may have left already. | It must have rained last night. | The cake must have burned.

name: Scalar Equative As … As
s: As ... as sets one thing's degree against another's without saying the first has more.
x: The new shelf is as wide as the old one. | The new shelf is as wide as the old one. | Max is as tall as his sister. | The new shelf is as wide as the old one. | Max is as tall as his sister. | The new shelf is as wide as the old one. | Max is as tall as his sister.

name: Evaluative Adjective with Of and an Infinitival

t.curious: Judging a person's action with "kind of you"
t.child: Judging a person's action with "kind of you"

s: A sentence like It was kind of you to call judges a person by what they did or considered doing.
p: Clause[dummy it + be + Adj + PP[of + NPᵢ] + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

t.curious: A noun of a noun, used to judge

s: In a phrase like a nitwit of a husband, the first noun is a judgment about the person or thing named by the second.
p: NP[... Nom₁ of NP₂], with Nom₁ predicated of the referent of NP₂
x: her stupid nitwit of a husband | wobbly jellies of men | that destroyer of education of a minister | her stupid nitwit of a husband | wobbly jellies of men | that destroyer of education of a minister | her stupid nitwit of a husband | wobbly jellies of men | that destroyer of education of a minister

name: Clause-Orientated Evaluative Adjunct

t.curious: Showing how you feel about what happened
t.child: Showing how you feel about what happened

s: An adverb such as fortunately can open a sentence and express the speaker's evaluation of what is reported.
p: evaluative AdvP + clause, often separated prosodically
x: Fortunately, the backup worked. | Fortunately, the backup worked. | Sadly, the party ended early. | Fortunately, the backup worked. | Sadly, the party ended early. | Fortunately, the backup worked. | Luckily, the rain stopped.

name: Concessive Conditional Even If
s: Even if names a condition that might seem to threaten a plan and says the plan holds anyway.

name: Every Inch with a Nominal Predicative

s: Every inch a philosopher says that someone fully fits a role or type, in the respects that matter for it.
x: She is every inch a philosopher. | She is every inch a philosopher. | He is every inch a gentleman. | She is every inch a leader. | She is every inch a philosopher. | He is every inch a gentleman.

name: Speech-Act or Evidential Because

t.curious: Giving your reason for saying something
t.child: Giving your reason for saying something

s: A because phrase can explain why the speaker says something, not why the thing happened.

name: Exclamation
s: An exclamation is an utterance that expresses strong feeling, and the way it's said is part of what makes it one.
p: Utterance with exclamatory prosody and heightened-stance force
x: Ouch! | What a lovely day! | A snake! | That's amazing! | Ouch! | What a lovely day! | A snake! | That's amazing! | Ouch! | What a lovely day! | A snake! | That's amazing!

name: Alternative Exhaustive Conditional

s: A whether phrase with two alternatives says the result holds on either one.

s: There plus be plus no plus an -ing verb presents an action as unavailable in the circumstances.

s: There plus be can introduce something, or say that it's present, available or going on.

name: Experiential Perfect

t.curious: Asking whether something has ever happened
t.child: Asking whether something has ever happened

s: A have plus past-participle sentence can place earlier happenings within a stretch of time that matters now.

name: Extended Existential with a Predicate
s: A there sentence can introduce something and then say where it is or what it's doing.

name: Spatial Extent with a Measure NP
s: After a verb of movement, a measured distance can answer the question "how far".

s: Some verbs treat what follows them as a fact, and the sentence keeps treating it that way even when it's negative.

name: Prepositional Passive

t.child: Verbs that go with a particular small word

name: Preterite with Present-Time Politeness

name: Finite Auxiliary with Not

name: Progressive Futurate

s: Some student or other introduces someone while leaving open who exactly it was.
p: NP[some + singular count Nom + or other]

name: Source Locative-Complement Construction
s: A small phrase with from, away, off or out can tell where a movement or change began.
x: She came from Toronto. | Ed emerged from under the car. | She walked away. | Kim jumped off the pier. | He came out of the room. | They flew from Toronto to Ottawa. | She came from Toronto. | Ed emerged from under the car. | She walked away. | Kim jumped off the pier. | He came out of the room. | They flew from Toronto to Ottawa.

name: Specificational Copular Clause

t.curious: Sentences that fill in an answer

s: Some sentences with is set up a description and then name what fits it.
x: The main obstacle is the permit. | The permit is the main obstacle. | The main obstacle is the permit. | The permit is the main obstacle. | The main obstacle is the permit. | The permit is the main obstacle.

name: Speech-Act Adverbial
s: An adverb like frankly can describe how or why the speaker is making the statement, not what the statement is about.
p: supplementary adverbial oriented to the utterance act
x: Frankly, the repair won’t last. | Frankly, the repair won't last. | Honestly, the soup needs salt. | Frankly, the repair won't last. | Honestly, the soup needs salt.

name: Aspectual Still and Negative Yet
s: Not yet and still place something against an expected course of events: one reports what hasn't happened, the other what carries on.
p: clause with still or polarity-sensitive yet and a temporal reference point
x: The alarm hasn’t stopped yet. | The alarm hasn't stopped yet. | The alarm is still ringing. | The alarm hasn't stopped yet. | The alarm is still ringing. | The kettle hasn't boiled yet. | The dog is still barking.

name: Exclamation with Stressed Some

t.curious: Exclaiming that something was quite a specimen

s: Said with heavy stress, some in an exclamation presents something as remarkable for its kind.
x: SOME hotel that was! An utter disgrace! | Those are SOME elephants! | That was SOME wine we drank! | SOME hotel that was! An utter disgrace! | Those are SOME elephants! | That was SOME wine we drank! | SOME hotel that was! An utter disgrace! | Those are SOME elephants! | That was SOME wine we drank!

name: Strong Proper Name Construction
s: Names like Kim and New York need no the, a or my in front of them, and some family words can work the same way.
p: NP[Head:Nom[sg]; no Det] with naming semantics, in referential use
x: Kim called. | She lives in New York. | Mom called. | You wanna roll the ball to Mommy? | Did you tell Grampa you went out to see him? | Poor Henry needs a rest. | Poor Mom needs a rest. | Kim called. | She lives in New York. | Mom called. | Poor Henry needs a rest. | Kim called.

name: Subject-Oriented Ascriptive Predicative
s: Some verbs link the subject to a word or phrase that tells you what the subject is like.
x: Jo seems unusually calm. | Jo seems unusually calm. | Jo is unusually calm. | Jo seems unusually calm. | Jo is unusually calm.

name: Subject Control in a To-Infinitival Complement
s: In some sentences, the person named at the start is also the one who does the action in the to-phrase.
p: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]
x: Jo promised to return. | Jo promised to return. | There seems to be a leak. | Jo promised to return.

name: Subject-determiner (Genitive NP)

t.curious: A genitive that acts like a subject

s: Sometimes the word with 's before a noun tells you who did the action the noun names, not who owns something.
x: Brett's use of the microphone | the committee's approval of the plan | Brett's use of the microphone | the committee's approval of the plan | Brett's use of the microphone | the committee's approval of the plan

name: Subject Extraposition

t.curious: Saving the clause for the end

s: A sentence can start with it and put a clause after the verb to say what the situation is.
p: Clause[Subject:dummy it + VP[... + extraposed content clause or infinitival]]
x: It worries me that he hasn’t phoned. | It is unclear why she told him. | It would be pointless to resist. | It worries me that he hasn't phoned. | It is unclear why she told him. | It would be pointless to resist. | It worries me that he hasn't phoned. | It is unclear why she told him. | It would be pointless to resist.

name: Subject-Linked Genitive Superlative
s: A verb followed by a genitive and a superlative, as in worked our hardest, says the effort reached its highest point.
x: Kate and I have worked our hardest to raise them that way. | They worked at their hardest. | They worked their hardest. | Kate and I have worked our hardest to raise them that way. | They worked at their hardest. | They worked their hardest. | Kate and I have worked our hardest to raise them that way. | They worked their hardest.

name: Subject Raising with a Catenative Verb

t.curious: Sentences where the subject belongs to the next verb

s: With verbs like seem, the subject of the sentence really belongs to the to-phrase that follows.
p: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]
x: There seems to be a leak. | Jo seems to have checked the lock. | There seems to be a leak. | Jo seems to have checked the lock. | The lock seems to have been checked by Jo. | There seems to be a leak. | Jo seems to have checked the lock.

name: Subject-Oriented Resultative

t.curious: Saying how the subject ends up
t.child: Saying how the subject ends up

s: A word after the verb can tell you what state the subject reaches, as in froze solid.
p: VP[Head:V + PredComp:XP predicated of the subject]
x: The basin froze solid. | The basin froze solid. | The pond froze solid. | The basin froze solid. | The basin froze solid. | The pond froze solid.

name: Mandative Subjunctive
s: After words like requested, a that-clause can use the plain form of the verb to say what is required or recommended.

name: Exemplifying Such As
s: Such as introduces some examples of the kind of thing you've just named.

name: Degree Such with Nominal and Result Clause

t.curious: Such a cold morning that the locks froze
t.child: Such a cold morning that the locks froze

s: Such plus a noun phrase can describe how extreme something was by giving what resulted from it.

name: Conditional Provided That
s: Provided that adds a condition under which a promise or permission holds.

name: Scalar Superlative with a Comparison Set

t.curious: The most extreme of a group
t.child: The most extreme of a group

s: A word like narrowest picks one item as the extreme within a set the speaker has in mind.
p: superlative AdjP/AdvP, optionally with of/in domain expression

name: Supplementary Appositive NP

t.curious: A second description added to a name

s: A second noun phrase beside the first adds another way of identifying the same person or thing.
p: anchor NP + supplementary NP with a co-referential interpretation
x: Lee, our treasurer, signed the form. | Lee, our treasurer, signed the form. | Lee signed the form. | Lee, our treasurer, signed the form.

name: Supplementary Relative

t.curious: A which clause that adds extra information

s: A which clause after a name can add a separate piece of information about it.

name: Deverbal Synthetic Noun Compound
s: In its agentive reading, a compound like window-cleaner names a person by the thing they work on and what they do.

s: The plus an adjective can stand for a class of people or an abstract domain, with no noun after it.

s: A title such as Sir or Dr can sit in front of a person's name, and the title helps decide which form of the name follows.
x: Sir James opened the ceremony. | Dr Patel wrote the report. | Sir James opened the ceremony. | Dr Patel wrote the report. | Sir James opened the ceremony. | Dr Patel wrote the report.

name: Excess Degree Too with an Infinitival
s: Too plus a describing word and an action can say that something goes past the limit that action sets.

t.child: Passing something to someone with to

s: Until names the point up to which something goes on, or before which something doesn't happen.

s: A name or title said directly to the person you're speaking to, set apart from the rest of the sentence.

s: A verb phrase is a verb together with the words that complete or modify it, not including the subject.

s: Some names include the word the as part of the name, as in the Thames.

name: Topic Proposal with What About
s: What about, followed by a thing or an action, puts something forward for the other person to think about.

s: What plus a noun description can express a feeling about something, with no verb at all.

name: What With Circumstantial Adjunct
s: What with and one or more circumstances offers them as the reason for what happened.

s: Why not plus an action suggests doing it, by asking whether there is any reason against.

name: With a Capital Letter Construction
s: Adding with a capital D (or another letter) to a word says how it is written, and can point to an official or named meaning.

s: Adding with a lowercase r (or another letter) says how a word is written, and can point to an ordinary meaning.
